name: Shillong
description: Capital city of Meghalaya and headquarters of East Khasi Hills district, known as the Scotland of the East for its rolling hills, pine forests, and colonial-era architecture. Serves as the main base for exploring waterfalls, caves, and living root bridges of the region.
facts: Capital and largest city of Meghalaya
Headquarters of East Khasi Hills district
Known for educational institutions and vibrant markets

name: Shillong Peak
description: Highest point in Meghalaya at approximately 1,965 m, offering panoramic views of Shillong city, the surrounding Khasi Hills, and on clear days the plains of Bangladesh. Sacred to the Khasi people as the abode of the deity U Shyllong.
facts: About 10 km south of Shillong city
Sacred site associated with Khasi deity U Shyllong
Offers views of city and distant plains

name: Elephant Falls
description: Multi-tiered waterfall on the outskirts of Shillong, originally named Ka Kshaid Lai Pateng Khohsiew (three-step waterfall). Easy access with steps and viewpoints; named after a rock formation resembling an elephant that was destroyed in the 1897 earthquake.
facts: About 12 km from Shillong city center

name: Nohkalikai Falls
description: Tallest plunge waterfall in India at about 340 m (1,115 ft), plunging from the Sohra plateau into a turquoise pool. Located near Sohra (Cherrapunji), one of the wettest places on Earth; associated with a local Khasi legend of Ka Likai.
facts: Highest plunge waterfall in India (~340 m)
Named after the legend of Ka Likai

name: Sohra (Cherrapunji)
description: Town on the southern edge of the East Khasi Hills plateau, historically one of the wettest places on Earth. Gateway to numerous waterfalls, caves, living root bridges, and panoramic views over the Bangladesh plains.
facts: One of the wettest places on Earth
Base for Nohkalikai Falls and Mawsmai Cave

name: Mawlynnong Village
description: Village in East Khasi Hills known as Asia’s cleanest village, awarded the tag by Discover India in 2003. Features traditional Khasi matrilineal culture, bamboo skywalks, balancing rocks, and proximity to living root bridges and the Bangladesh border.
facts: Awarded Cleanest Village in Asia in 2003
Features bamboo skywalk and balancing rock

name: Double Decker Living Root Bridge (Nongriat)
description: Unique two-tier living root bridge formed from the aerial roots of Ficus elastica trees by Khasi villagers in Nongriat village. Reached by a steep trek of about 3,000–3,500 steps from Tyrna; a remarkable example of indigenous bioengineering.
facts: Only double-decker living root bridge of its kind
Lower bridge estimated over 180 years old

name: Mawsmai Cave
description: Accessible limestone show cave near Sohra with illuminated passages, stalactites, and stalagmites. One of the first show caves in Meghalaya, formed by dissolution of limestone in the high-rainfall Khasi Hills.
facts: Length of accessible section around 150–250 m
Khasi name means Oath Stone Cave

name: Laitlum Canyon
description: Dramatic canyon and viewpoint about 25 km from Shillong, offering sweeping views of deep green valleys and ridges. Often called the Grand Canyon of Meghalaya; popular for photography and short walks.
facts: About 25 km from Shillong via Smit
Name means end of the hills

name: Mawphlang Sacred Forest
description: Ancient sacred grove (Law Lyngdoh) near Mawphlang village, preserved for centuries by Khasi traditions as the abode of deities. Features old-growth forest, monoliths, and high biodiversity; visitors may not remove anything from the forest.
facts: Protected by traditional Khasi beliefs for centuries

name: Nohsngithiang Falls (Seven Sisters Falls)
description: Segmented waterfall near Mawsmai, dropping about 315 m over limestone cliffs in seven streams during the rainy season. Offers dramatic views of the falls and the Bangladesh plains below.
facts: Also known as Seven Sisters Falls
Best viewed in full flow during monsoon

name: Don Bosco Centre for Indigenous Cultures
description: Museum in Mawlai, Shillong, showcasing the indigenous cultures of Northeast India across seven floors and 17 galleries. Features artefacts, musical instruments, traditional housing, and a rooftop viewpoint.
